text: A call uses one GPU: the one its arrays live on (plans, graphs and reductions follow their planes; a JAX function runs on the JAX device it was built under, one function per GPU). Arrays on two GPUs in one call are refused by name.
way_out: put the arrays on the GPU you want

text: eagle works in each GPU's primary context, the one CuPy, torch, JAX and Warp share; memory or streams from a context you created yourself are outside our scope.
Inputs of another float type are converted to float64, which is a copy (our scope here): pass float64 arrays to avoid it.

A call runs the float32 or the float64 build, chosen by its first float plane, and mixing them is refused (the kernel is built once per dtype). JAX itself is float32 unless `jax_enable_x64` is on: cast every plane to one dtype, or turn x64 on as this page does.
way_out: cast planes to one dtype, or enable x64

text: `vmap` over a batch of `Param` values is one launch over every entry; a kernel that reduces over samples itself, or has a `jump=` plan, runs one launch per entry instead (our scope): put the varying value in a plane for one launch.
way_out: put the varying value in a plane

text: `jax.export` modules carry the kernel's digest, not its code (so they stay small and cache-friendly): in a fresh process call `eagle.frameworks.jax.preload(cache_dir)` before running one.
`Terminated` is a stop decision, not a number, so it carries no derivative and a finished sample's derivatives are zero. Keep any soft version of the decision in `jnp`, and differentiate the planes.
way_out: keep a soft version in jnp

text: Needs `jax>=0.11.2`, the release whose XLA FFI version the bridge is built against (our scope); a newer jax works.
`torch.compile` needs torch 2.4 or newer, the release that added the custom-op API the bridge uses; on an older torch run the step eagerly.

Inside a `torch.compile` region only first-order reverse mode runs, because compile traces the backward once, ahead of time (torch's design); run forward AD and double backward outside it, or through `torch.func`.
way_out: run them outside the compiled region, or through torch.func

text: A kernel that finishes its own samples returns a fresh `Terminated` mask and leaves yours untouched (our design, so inputs are never written); keep the returned mask as the next step's.

`torch.func.vmap` over a batch of `Param` values is one launch over every entry; a kernel with a `jump=` plan runs one launch per entry instead (our scope): put the varying value in a plane for one launch.
way_out: put the varying value in a plane

text: No gradients through NumPy or CuPy, because neither has autodiff (the frameworks' design): write the vjp yourself and pass it as `vjps=` (see [the graph model](../userguide/graph_model)), or use the [torch](torch.ipynb) or [JAX](jax.ipynb) bridge.
way_out: write the vjp, or use the torch or JAX bridge

text: `until_done` never writes a JAX or torch array (our design: your arrays stay yours): take the answer from `Runner.result(name)`, a new array of your framework. A NumPy or CuPy plane is still written in place.
`until_done` refuses a host plane beside a device plane, by name (our scope): move one side, so that every plane is on the host or every plane is on the device.
The CPU host runs float32 plugins, but not yet the ones with integer mutables, a `Terminated` mask or derivative kernels (our scope): use float64 for those on the host, or the GPU.
way_out: float64 on the host, or the GPU

text: NumPy calls block until the result is ready, because host arrays have no stream (NumPy's design); CuPy arrays run asynchronously.
way_out: use CuPy arrays for asynchronous work

text: `plan.run` does not follow a CuPy stream you opened (our scope): bind the arrays and call `bind(...).launch()` as above to stay ordered on it.
Warp kernels cannot call an eagle kernel, because a Warp kernel is device code and an eagle launch is a call from Python (their design): launch eagle between your Warp launches.
Planes are component-major, `(3, n)` for a vector, so arrays of Warp vector types (`wp.vec3d`) are refused (our scope): pass a `(3, n)` array.

Gradients are reverse mode only: `Tape.record_func`, which records eagle's backward, has no forward mode and no second derivative (Warp's design): differentiate once with `tape.backward`, or use the [JAX](jax.ipynb) bridge for forward mode and higher orders.
way_out: differentiate once, or the JAX bridge

text: A call runs the float32 or the float64 build, chosen by its first float array, and mixing them is refused (the kernel is built once per dtype, our scope): create every array in one float dtype.

A kernel is built on its first call, and a graph capture records device work only, so a build cannot happen inside one (CUDA's design): call `fn.prepare(mode, device)` (or the function once) before `wp.capture_begin`.

Warp keeps one global tape, creates its CUDA context on first use and holds the current stream per device, not per thread (Warp's design), so threads pass `tape=` to each call, the device is touched once (`wp.zeros(1, device=device)`) before they start, and CUDA `.numpy()`, `ScopedStream` and `set_stream` are not called from several threads at once: read back on one thread, or copy with an explicit stream.
way_out: tape= per call, touch the device first, read back on one thread

text: In a recorded loop a node runs before the plan, preparing the step from the current state (our design): write the step as `[node, plan]`. The run calls the node on the initial state before step 0; applying it once more after the last step is yours, and your framework's autograd of that call gives the seeds.
In a recorded loop the node's vjp is a callable run host-synchronized once per step (our scope): a `Node` as the vjp is refused by name. A hooked reverse costs what your model costs per step.

A torch module that allocates cannot be captured as a plain `opaque`, because torch hands its graph memory to the next replay (torch's design): capture it with `torch.cuda.CUDAGraph(keep_graph=True)` and insert it with `child`, or write it with `out=`.
A stream or host node cannot run inside a stepping loop's device graph (our scope): capture it (`opaque(fn)`, or `child`), or call `runner.run()` with `max_steps=k`, then your code, in your own loop.
way_out: capture it, or your own run(max_steps=k) loop

text: An eagle graph is not launched inside `torch.cuda.graph` or `wp.capture_begin` (our design: one owner of the streams and syncs, and the call is refused by name). Go the other way: hand your torch `CUDAGraph` or Warp graph to eagle with `child(graph, reads=..., writes=...)`, and one eagle launch runs the whole thing (section 6, torch model inside an eagle batch).
A NumPy function in a GPU graph is host-synchronized, because host arrays have no stream (NumPy's design): write it as `opaque(fn, eager=True)`, or use CuPy for work that stays on the device.
JAX cannot run inside a captured eagle graph or stepping loop, because XLA owns its allocations (XLA's design): use `eagle.frameworks.jax.node` between launches, or put the batch inside `jit`.
JAX leaves its last GPU current; eagle follows your arrays, so only NEW cupy allocations are affected (cupy allocates on the current device): make them inside `with cupy.cuda.Device(n):`.

On CUDA 13, CuPy cannot compile a kernel after JAX has started, because JAX loads NVIDIA's NVRTC library first and that build of it cannot find its own builtins (NVIDIA's and JAX's packaging): call `cupy.cuda.nvrtc.getVersion()` before your first JAX call, as the notebooks here do.
`jax.grad` does not differentiate through `lax.while_loop` (JAX's rule): use `lax.scan` with a next-state kernel.

On a GPU a JAX node runs between launches, not inside `until_done`'s one device graph, because XLA owns its own memory and cannot be captured (XLA's design): drive the graph with your own loop, as this page does, or put the batch inside `jit` (tutorial 18).
way_out: own launch loop, or the batch inside jit

text: `jax.grad` does not go through `lax.while_loop`, because the trip count is only known at run time (JAX's rule): use `lax.scan` with a fixed length for gradients, as this page does.

Compaction, conditionals and event refinement belong to `until_done`; inside `jit` the loop is XLA's (`while_loop`, `scan`), so they do not apply there (XLA's design): use `until_done` when you need them.
JAX runs under free-threading on Python 3.14t only, because jaxlib publishes no 3.13t wheel (JAX's release choice): use 3.14t for free-threaded JAX, or a regular 3.13 build.
torch's CPU wheels cover free-threaded Python 3.14t only, none for 3.13t (torch's release choice): use 3.14t for free-threaded torch, or a regular 3.13 build.
cupy and torch publish no Python 3.15 wheels yet (their release choice), so the CuPy and torch interop tests skip on 3.15: use Python 3.14 for them.

Before NumPy 2.2, every array NumPy imports through DLPack is read-only (NumPy's behavior), so a NumPy view of an eagle buffer cannot be written: write through the original array, or use NumPy 2.2 or later.

A `buffer=` array made inside a device loop or branch is not a gradient key, because the body rewrites it every turn and no one array is its value (our scope): make the `buffer=` outside the body, or seed `result`.

A `record=True` loop body holds kernel launches only: a `break`, `continue`, `if`/`elif`/`else` or `match` inside it is refused (our scope): keep the control flow outside the recorded loop, or build with `record=False`.
An uncapped `while cell:` cannot be recorded with `record=True` (our scope): cap it with `for _ in range(N): if not cell: break`.
A recorded loop that reads one array under two names is refused (our scope): pass it under one name.

IF/ELSE and SWITCH conditional nodes need an NVIDIA driver that supports CUDA 12.8 (SWITCH: driver 570); on an older driver eagle builds the same arms from plain IF nodes, with one extra node for the decision, and the results are the same (the driver's feature): update the driver for the single nodes.
